parts.title: Booking an airport transfer
parts.context: A man books a taxi to meet his family at the airport.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a transfer company to book a taxi from the airport. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: gina
script.text: Prime Transfers, Gina speaking.

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: Hello. I'd like to book a taxi to meet us at the airport when we arrive, please. We're coming for a family holiday.

script.speaker: gina
script.text: Certainly. I'll take some details.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The taxi is to meet them at the airport, so 'airport' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: gina
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: Oliver Bannister. That's B-A-N-N-I-S-T-E-R.

script.speaker: gina
script.text: Thank you, Mr Bannister. Which airport will you arrive at?

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: Gatwick.

script.speaker: gina
script.text: And on which date?

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: The third of March.

script.speaker: gina
script.text: What time does your flight land?

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: It's scheduled to land at three, but the airline says it often arrives late, so say four to be safe.

script.speaker: gina
script.text: How many passengers will there be?

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: Three, my wife, our daughter and me.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: gina
script.text: And where would you like to be taken?

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: To the Regent Hotel, in the centre of Brighton. I have the address here.

script.speaker: gina
script.text: That's fine. How much luggage will you have?

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: Four large suitcases, and some hand luggage. Is that a problem?

script.speaker: gina
script.text: Not at all. We'll send a people carrier, which has plenty of room. The fare is sixty-five pounds, and that includes the tolls.

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: That's good. How will we find the driver?

script.speaker: gina
script.text: He'll be waiting in the arrivals hall, holding a sign with your name on it. If you can't see him, you can call the number on your confirmation.

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: What if the flight is delayed?

script.speaker: gina
script.text: We track all flights, so we'll know. And there's thirty minutes of free waiting time after landing, which is enough for most people to collect their luggage.

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: Wonderful. I'll pay by card now.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A company induction day
parts.context: A manager explains the programme of an induction day.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a manager explaining the programme of an induction day for new employees. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: fraser
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Halden Engineering. I'm Neil Fraser, the personnel manager, and I'll explain how today will work. You'll attend five sessions, in different parts of the building, so please keep your map with you.

script.speaker: fraser
script.text: The first session is health and safety, which is compulsory for everyone. It's in the main hall, because it's the largest room, and it includes a short fire drill.

script.speaker: fraser
script.text: Then you'll go to the IT office, where you'll receive your computer account and your email address. Please have your passwords ready, because it takes a while if you forget them.

script.speaker: fraser
script.text: After lunch, there's a session on the history of the company, in the boardroom. It's more interesting than it sounds, and the chief executive will join us to answer your questions.

script.speaker: fraser
script.text: Later, you'll meet your own teams in the canteen, over coffee and cakes, which is a relaxed way to meet your new colleagues. And finally, you'll visit the human resources office, where we'll explain your pension and other benefits.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: fraser
script.text: Some practical points. Normal working hours start at half past eight, but today you needn't come so early, because we're starting at nine.

script.speaker: fraser
script.text: Lunch breaks are flexible. You can take them whenever it suits your team, between twelve and two, as long as you take one full hour.

script.speaker: fraser
script.text: The dress code is smart casual. You don't need a suit or a tie, but we ask you not to wear jeans or trainers when you meet visitors from other companies.

script.speaker: fraser
script.text: All new staff have a probation period of six months, during which your manager will review your progress each month, and we'll talk about how you're getting on.

script.speaker: fraser
script.text: If you have a problem, the first person to talk to is your line manager, not the personnel office. Only if the problem is about your line manager, should you come to us. Now, let's make a start.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: An experiment on mould
parts.context: Two biology students plan an experiment on mould growth.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two biology students, Poppy and Eli, planning an experiment on mould. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: poppy
script.text: Eli, let's agree on the plan for the mould experiment. What's the aim, exactly?

script.speaker: eli
script.text: To find out how temperature affects the growth of mould. Our hypothesis is that it will grow faster in a warm place than in a cold one.

script.speaker: poppy
script.text: And we chose bread because?

script.speaker: eli
script.text: It's cheap, and mould grows quickly on it, so we can see results within days. We don't have a lot of time.

script.speaker: poppy
script.text: What about safety? Some moulds can cause allergies.

script.speaker: eli
script.text: That's why we seal each dish in a bag, and we never open them. We wear gloves when we handle the bags, and we dispose of them afterwards.

script.speaker: poppy
script.text: How long will the experiment last?

script.speaker: eli
script.text: A week. Dr Ward said that's enough to see a difference, and any longer would be pointless.

script.speaker: poppy
script.text: And what do you predict?

script.speaker: eli
script.text: That the mould in the warm room will grow much faster, perhaps twice as fast as in the fridge.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: poppy
script.text: Let's write the method. First, put a slice of bread in a clean dish.

script.speaker: eli
script.text: Then add a few drops of water, because mould needs moisture to grow.

script.speaker: poppy
script.text: Seal each dish in a plastic bag, so that no spores can escape.

script.speaker: eli
script.text: We put one bag in a warm room, and the other in the fridge, and we leave both undisturbed.

script.speaker: poppy
script.text: Every day, we measure the area covered by mould with a ruler, and note the result.

script.speaker: eli
script.text: I'll keep the table of results, and you can take photographs.

script.speaker: poppy
script.text: Fine. We'll start tomorrow.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the history of cinema
parts.context: A lecture on cinema from the Lumière brothers to streaming.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the history of cinema. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Today we'll look at the history of cinema, which is only a little more than a hundred and twenty years old, and yet has become one of the most powerful forms of entertainment.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Moving pictures were invented by several people at about the same time. In America, Thomas Edison's company developed a machine that one person at a time could watch through a peephole. But the first film shown to a paying audience was projected by the Lumière brothers in Paris, in December eighteen ninety-five. Their films were very short, lasting less than a minute, and showed everyday scenes, such as workers leaving a factory.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Early films were silent, but cinemas were never quiet. They employed live music, usually a pianist, who played along with the action, and some larger cinemas had a whole orchestra.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The French magician Georges Méliès realised that film could do more than record reality. In his famous film, A Trip to the Moon, from nineteen oh two, he used special effects, such as stopping the camera and changing the scene, to create fantasy.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Soon the centre of the industry moved to the United States, and in particular to a suburb of Los Angeles in California called Hollywood, where the weather was sunny and the land cheap.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The next great change was sound. The Jazz Singer, in nineteen twenty-seven, was the first feature film with synchronised speech, and within a few years, silent films had almost disappeared. Colour followed in the nineteen thirties, using a process called Technicolor, and it was spectacular in films such as The Wizard of Oz.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: In the nineteen fifties, television reduced cinema audiences, and studios responded with wider screens and bigger spectacles. The next revolution was digital. In nineteen ninety-five, Toy Story became the first feature film made entirely with computer animation.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Today many people watch films on streaming services, at home or on a phone, and the future of the cinema is a subject of lively debate. Next week we'll look at the history of television.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
